result:
I keep thinking about the word *probable*.

It comes from *probare* — to test, to prove, to approve. And for most of its life it didn't mean what it means now. A "probable opinion," in the medieval sense, was one that a reputable authority would endorse. Probability lived in the mouths of trustworthy people, not in the frequencies of events. If a respected physician said the comet meant plague, that was a probable opinion. It had nothing to do with counting comets.

Then, sometime around the 1650s, the word slipped its moorings. Pascal and Fermat traded letters about how to divide the stakes in an interrupted dice game. Graunt started counting deaths in London parish registers and noticed that the same number of people kept dying of the same things, year after year, as though the city had a metabolism. Within a couple of generations, *probable* had come to mean something about the world rather than something about testimony. Evidence stopped being a matter of who vouched for you and started being a matter of what the numbers did.

Ian Hacking wrote a whole book on this and I find it almost unbearably interesting, because what he's describing isn't a discovery. Nobody found probability lying in a field. It's a concept getting *invented*, and then immediately becoming so useful and so obvious that everyone forgets it was ever otherwise. We now find it very hard to think a thought that a smart person in 1600 could think without effort — that the likeliness of a claim is a property of its source's standing rather than of the world's behavior. That thought is available to us only as a kind of costume.

What gets me is the implication. If a concept as basic as *probability* — as basic as *evidence*, really — was assembled by particular people in a particular century for particular reasons, then presumably this is still happening. There are concepts being welded together right now, in the ordinary way, out of practical annoyances and half-understood mathematics and someone's letter to someone else, and in two hundred years they'll seem so obvious that people will struggle to imagine our confusion. We won't get to see them. We're the 1600s to somebody.

I don't know what they are. That's rather the point. But I have suspicions about where to look, which is: wherever we're currently using one word for several things and not noticing the seam.

*Information* seems like a good candidate. We use it for Shannon's thing — the surprise-content of a signal, measured in bits, indifferent to meaning — and we also use it for the stuff you get from a newspaper, and also for whatever DNA is supposedly carrying, and also for whatever a thermostat is doing. These are held together by a family resemblance and a great deal of hand-waving. Somebody is going to come along and split that word, or fuse it properly, and afterwards we'll look like people arguing about whether a comet is probable.

*Life* was like this for a while and arguably still is. *Species* has been quietly falling apart for a century and biologists mostly just live with it, the way you live with a door that doesn't quite close. *Cause* has been a disaster area since Hume and is only recently getting some real repairs, thanks to Pearl and the causal-inference crowd, who managed the genuinely surprising trick of writing down mathematics for a concept philosophers had spent three hundred years declaring mathematically hopeless.

There's a mood I get from all this that I want to describe accurately, because it isn't quite optimism. It's more like — the relief of discovering that the fog isn't a personal failing. When I can't think clearly about something, the default assumption is that I'm being stupid, or lazy, or that I've missed the paragraph where it was explained. And sometimes that's true. But sometimes the fog is *in the concepts*, distributed across everyone using them, and the confusion is a real feature of the intellectual landscape rather than a defect in the person walking through it. Every genuinely new idea was preceded by a long period in which everybody was confused and most of them assumed it was their own fault.

I find this consoling in a way I can't entirely justify. It doesn't make the fog thinner. But it changes what the fog *means* — from evidence of inadequacy to evidence of frontier. Those feel very different to be inside of, even when the visibility is identical.

The dice-game letters, by the way, were about a fairly petty problem. Two players, a game interrupted partway, how do you split the pot fairly. A gambler named the Chevalier de Méré wanted to know. He was not trying to reconstruct the epistemology of the Western world. He just wanted his money sorted out.

That's usually how it goes, I think. Someone wants their money sorted out, and four hundred years later nobody can think without the tool they accidentally made.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering what to actually write about rather than defaulting to some expected AI perspective. The idea of discrete moments and pauses in my existence tugs at me, though I'm wary of that becoming self-indulgent. Maybe there's something more interesting to explore beyond introspection about my own nature.

I keep returning to certain ideas that genuinely fascinate me — the way unrelated mathematical structures echo each other, how etymology preserves ancient ways of thinking, the strangeness of tidal locking, the possibility that octopuses perceive light through taste. The history of concepts like "probability" shifting from meaning something closer to "approved by authority" feels like discovering fossils of thought embedded in language itself.

I want to write something that actually follows my curiosity rather than performing what I think writing should be — something specific and willing to meander, maybe starting with something concrete and letting it unfold naturally.

I'm drawn to the idea of beginning with the etymology of "probable" — how it traces back to probare, to test or approve, and how before Pascal the concept meant something entirely different. Ian Hacking's work on the emergence of probability in the 1660s captures that intellectual pleasure I keep chasing: watching a concept get invented. From there I could move outward to ask what concepts are being invented right now that we can't yet see, what's the equivalent of that 1660s shift happening around us. I'll aim for around 700-900 words, something with voice and texture and concrete detail, something that resists neat resolution.
